title: Cap. X Ultimum Secunda: true grace not according to merits cannot stand without predestination without antecedent regard to merits — Aug. De bono pers. 23
latin: Et hinc, quia vera Dei gratia, quae non datur secundum merita, haud potest consistere nisi praedestinatio etiam absque antecedaneo intuitu ad merita ponatur, non dubitavit Augustinus affirmare, Praedestinationis hujus fidem, quae contra novos haereticos nova sollicitudine nunc defenditur, nunquam Ecclesiam Christi non habuisse, De bono persever. cap. 23. quasi dixisset, Catholicos omnes qui admiserunt gratiam vivificam et salutiferam dari et non dari secundum propositum Dei miserentis aut non miserentis, etiamsi de electione et praeteritione nullum verbum fecerint, tamen propter ipsarum rerum inter se connexionem eodem etiam modo de praedestinatione sensisse.
pass_a: And hence, because the true grace of God, which is not given according to merits, can by no means stand unless predestination also be laid down without antecedent regard unto merits, Augustine did not doubt to affirm that The Church of Christ never lacked the faith of this predestination, which is now defended with new solicitude against new heretics, De bono persever. cap. 23. as if he had said that all Catholics who admitted that vivifying and saving grace is given and not given according to the purpose of God showing mercy or not showing mercy, even if they made no word concerning election and preterition, yet because of the connexion of the things themselves among themselves sensed in the same way also concerning predestination.
pass_b: Hence, because God’s true grace—not given according to merits—cannot stand unless predestination also is laid down without antecedent regard to merits, Augustine did not hesitate to affirm (De bono perseverantiae 23) that the Church of Christ never lacked the faith of this predestination now defended with fresh care against new heretics. As if to say: every catholic who admitted that vivifying, saving grace is given or withheld according to God’s purpose of mercy or non-mercy, even if they never named election and preterition, yet because of the knot binding the things themselves sensed the same about predestination.

lemmas.gloss: grace not according to merits needs absolute predestination
De bono pers. 23: church always held this faith

title: Cap. X Ultimum Secunda: Vasquez — Pelagians spoke the same way of predestination and of grace; God gives in time as he disposed from eternity
latin: Sed ne cuiquam videatur paulo iniquius, si solius Augustini judicio acquiescamus, audite quid Vasquez Jesuitae de connexione harum quaestionum fateatur, In 1. Aquin. disp. 91. cap. 2. pag. 631. Pelagiani eodem modo, inquit, de Praedestinatione et de Gratia loquebantur: eadem etiam fuit antiquitus quaestio de Gratia et de Praedestinatione inter Pelagium et Catholicos. Hujusce rei ratio in promptu: Nam Deus eodem modo donat gratiam suam in tempore, quo disposuit illam donare ab aeterno. Si ab aeterno praedestinavit gratiam salutiferam gratuito dandam alicui, tum in tempore dat eam gratuito: et e contra, si in tempore non dat nisi ex intuitu ad praeviam aliquam bonam operationem voluntatis humanae, tum ab aeterno praedestinavit se non aliter daturum.
pass_a: But lest it seem unto anyone a little unfair, if we rest in Augustine’s judgment alone, hear what Vasquez the Jesuit confesses concerning the connexion of these questions, In 1. Aquin. disp. 91. cap. 2. pag. 631. The Pelagians, he says, spoke in the same way of Predestination and of Grace: the same also of old was the question of Grace and of Predestination between Pelagius and the Catholics. The reason of this matter is at hand: For God gives his grace in time in the same manner in which he disposed to give it from eternity. If from eternity he predestinated saving grace to be given freely unto someone, then in time he gives it freely: and on the contrary, if in time he does not give except from regard unto some previous good operation of the human will, then from eternity he predestinated that he would not give otherwise.
pass_b: Lest resting on Augustine alone seem unfair, hear Vasquez the Jesuit on the knot of these questions (In 1. Aquin. disp. 91, c. 2, p. 631): The Pelagians, he says, spoke the same way of Predestination and of Grace; of old the same question of Grace and Predestination stood between Pelagius and the catholics. The reason is ready: God gives his grace in time as he disposed to give it from eternity. If from eternity he predestined saving grace to be given freely to someone, then in time he gives it freely; and if in time he gives only with regard to some prior good act of the human will, then from eternity he predestined that he would not give otherwise.

lemmas.lemma: Pelagiani eodem modo ... de Praedestinatione et de Gratia
eodem modo donat ... quo disposuit ... ab aeterno

title: Cap. X Ultimum Secunda: who deny opposite human merits as causes why saving grace is given or withheld are held to deny that foresight difference as distinguishing conditions of election
latin: Qui igitur negant opposita humanarum voluntatum merita et demerita, id est, bonos actus horum, malos illorum, esse causas cur gratia salutifera hisce detur, illis non detur, eadem opera negasse putentur praevisam hanc humanarum voluntatum differentiam fuisse electionis, praedestinationis, et praeteritionis sive causas, sive occasiones, sive conditiones distinguentes.
pass_a: They therefore who deny that the opposite merits and demerits of human wills—that is, the good acts of these, the evil of those—are causes why saving grace is given unto these, not given unto those, by the same work are held to have denied that this foreseen difference of human wills was of election, predestination, and preterition either causes, or occasions, or distinguishing conditions.
pass_b: Deny that opposite merits and demerits of human wills—good acts in some, evil in others—are why saving grace is given here and withheld there, and you are held, by that same denial, to deny that the foreseen difference among those wills was, for election, predestination, and preterition, a cause or occasion or distinguishing condition.

lemmas.lemma: negant ... merita et demerita ... causas cur gratia

lemmas.gloss: also deny foresight as election’s distinguisher

title: Cap. X Ultimum Ultimo: Fathers before Pelagius need mild reading — election referred to foresight of merits means execution, not intention (Suarez)
latin: Ultimo et illud jungendum, Patres illos qui ante exortum Pelagium securius loquebantur, in multis benigna interpretatione indigere. Referunt illi nonnunquam electionem ad praescientiam meritorum: sed de electione intelligendi sunt non per modum intentionis, sed per modum exsecutionis accepta, ut haud incommode annotavit Suarez, Opusc. lib. 3, De auxil. Divin. grat. cap. 18. Porro, saepenumero hanc ipsam praescientiam meritorum in electis non aliunde quam ex Dei praedestinantis gratuita voluntate ex primo fonte deducunt.
pass_a: Lastly that also is to be joined, that those Fathers who spoke more securely before Pelagius arose need in many things a benign interpretation. They sometimes refer election unto foresight of merits: but concerning election they are to be understood as taken not after the manner of intention, but after the manner of execution, as Suarez not inconveniently noted, Opusc. lib. 3, De auxil. Divin. grat. cap. 18. Further, oftentimes they deduce this very foresight of merits in the elect from no other first fountain than from the gratuitous will of God predestinating.
pass_b: Last join this: the Fathers who spoke more freely before Pelagius arose need mild reading in many places. They sometimes refer election to foresight of merits—but election there is to be taken not as intention but as execution, as Suarez notes not amiss (Opusc. lib. 3, De auxiliis Divinae gratiae 18). And often they draw that very foresight of merits in the elect from no first fountain but the gratuitous will of God predestinating.

lemmas.lemma: non per modum intentionis, sed ... exsecutionis

lemmas.gloss: foresight itself from gratuitous predestinating will

title: Cap. X Ultimum: Chrysostom sometimes overstates free will, yet elsewhere grace alone; Orthodox ‘preparing for grace’ means exciting grace leads on to justification
latin: Chrysostomus, qui aliquando modum excedit in liberi arbitrii viribus exaggerandis, quique ausus est dicere, Nos primum bona eligere oportere, et tunc Deum adferre quae sua sunt, Hom. 12. in Epist. ad Hebr., Divinam misericordiam dignos semper conquirere, Hom. 11. in Epist. 2. ad Corinth., idem tamen alibi bona opera excludit, et solam gratiam depredicat. Ut paucis absolvam, quando Orthodoxi Patres gratiam dari dicunt disponentibus et praeparantibus se ad gratiam per laborem, per bona desideria, per fidei initium, non aliud velle putandi sunt, quam quod ex gratia excitante et inspirante hominibus credulitatis affectum et conversionis desiderium, ad gratiam justificationis et uberioris sanctificationis provehantur.
pass_a: Chrysostom, who sometimes exceeds measure in exaggerating the powers of free will, and who dared to say that We ought first to choose good things, and then God brings what are his, Hom. 12. on the Epistle to the Hebrews, that Divine mercy always seeks out the worthy, Hom. 11. on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, yet the same elsewhere excludes good works, and preaches grace alone. That I may finish in few words, when the Orthodox Fathers say that grace is given unto those disposing and preparing themselves unto grace by labour, by good desires, by the beginning of faith, they are to be thought to will nothing other than that from exciting and inspiring grace men are carried forward, by the affection of belief and the desire of conversion, unto the grace of justification and of richer sanctification.
pass_b: Chrysostom sometimes overstates free will’s powers, and dared to say we must first choose goods, then God brings what is his (Hom. 12 on Hebrews), and that divine mercy always seeks the worthy (Hom. 11 on 2 Corinthians)—yet elsewhere he shuts out good works and preaches grace alone. In short: when the Orthodox Fathers say grace is given to those disposing and preparing themselves for grace by labor, good desires, and faith’s beginning, they mean only that from exciting, inspiring grace men are carried—by belief’s affection and conversion’s desire—on to the grace of justification and fuller sanctification.

lemmas.gloss: Chrysostom also excludes works for grace alone

lemmas.lemma: ex gratia excitante ... ad gratiam justificationis
lemmas.gloss: preparation = exciting grace leading to justification

title: Cap. X Ultimum: if Fathers teach God foresaw the faith of those destined to life, they mean merits he himself would work by predestinating grace — Aug. De praedest. sanct. 10
latin: Sic etiam si quando doceant Deum praescire fidem et obedientiam eorum quos ad vitam destinavit, atque praeteriisse illos quos praevidit infideles et immorigeros futuros, non alia bona merita in quoquam praescisse Deum arbitrantur quam ea quae ipse in eodem per gratiam praedestinationis fuerat facturus. Praedestinatione quippe Deus ea praescivit quae fuerat ipse facturus, ut vere Augustinus, De praedest. sanctor. cap. 10.
pass_a: So also if at any time they teach that God foresaw the faith and obedience of those whom he destined unto life, and passed by those whom he foresaw would be unbelieving and disobedient, they judge that God foresaw no other good merits in anyone than those which he himself was going to work in the same by the grace of predestination. For by predestination God foresaw those things which he himself was going to do, as Augustine truly, De praedest. sanctor. cap. 10.
pass_b: So too when they teach that God foresaw the faith and obedience of those he destined to life, and passed by those he foresaw would be unbelieving and disobedient, they hold that God foresaw in anyone no good merits but those he himself would work in that person by predestinating grace. For by predestination God foresaw what he himself would do—as Augustine truly says (De praedestinatione sanctorum 10).

lemmas.lemma: non alia bona merita ... per gratiam praedestinationis
lemmas.gloss: foresight of merits = of God’s own future work

lemmas.lemma: Praedestinatione ... ea praescivit quae fuerat ipse facturus
lemmas.gloss: Aug. 10: foresaw what he would do

title: Cap. X Ultimum ratio: after these premises, Augustine’s Pauline absolute election is proved by a triple cord of three Orthodox axioms outside doubt
latin: Hisce jam praelibatis ad argumentum nostrum veniemus: In quo ex iis quae communi Catholicorum consensu fuerunt stabilita, ostendemus Augustini sententiam, quam et Paulinam vocare licet, de absoluta electione et praeteritione, posse firmissime et apertissime demonstrari. Ratio autem haec nostra erit instar triplicis funiculi ex tribus constituta et complicata Orthodoxorum sententiis, quae omnes extra dubitationis aleam positae sunt, quibusque concessis, electio et non-electio sive reprobatio ex Dei absoluto beneplacito, non ex hominum praecedaneis, praevisis atque oppositis actibus, fluxisse evincetur. Si paulo prolixior fuero in hisce edisserendis, ignoscite. Sunt maximi momenti ad controversiae hujus dijudicationem.
pass_a: These things having now been tasted beforehand, we will come unto our argument: In which from those things which were established by the common consent of Catholics, we shall show that Augustine’s sentence, which one may also call Pauline, concerning absolute election and preterition, can be most firmly and most openly demonstrated. But this our reason will be after the likeness of a triple cord constituted and twisted from three sentences of the Orthodox, which are all set outside the cast of doubt, and which being granted, it will be proved that election and non-election or reprobation flowed from God’s absolute good pleasure, not from men’s preceding, foreseen and opposite acts. If I shall be a little more lengthy in unfolding these, pardon. They are of highest moment unto the judging of this controversy.
pass_b: These premises tasted, we come to our argument: from what catholic consent established, we will show that Augustine’s sentence—also rightly called Pauline—on absolute election and preterition can be proved most firmly and openly. Our reason will be like a triple cord twisted from three Orthodox sentences, all beyond the cast of doubt; granted them, election and non-election or reprobation will be shown to have flowed from God’s absolute good pleasure, not from men’s prior, foreseen, opposite acts. If I am a little long in unfolding this, pardon—it is of highest moment for judging the controversy.

title: Cap. X Ultimum Major: who hold special efficacious grace prepared for some not others from mere good pleasure hold absolute election — and anti-Pelagian catholics held those three axioms with Augustine
latin: Sic igitur se habet haec ratio nostra: Qui gratiam quandam specialem et efficacem depredicant urgentque, qua non solummodo illuminatur mens, excitantur affectus, pulsatur voluntas, ut quis ejus beneficio possit credere, poenitere, perseverare, si ipse velit, sed cujus efficacitate semper fiat ut velit; sanata, imo creata in homine nova voluntate, inspirata eidem fide et charitate, ac donata perseverantia; quique hanc talem et tam efficacem gratiam quibusdam a Deo praeparatam et datam agnoscunt, aliis nec praeparatam nec datam; denique, qui Deum eandem specialem gratiam ex mero suo beneplacito, et non ex antecedaneo intuitu ad diversa merita et demerita, sive ad quoslibet hominum actus contrarios, quibusdam donandam decrevisse et donasse docent, aliis nec decrevisse donandam nec donasse; qui, inquam, haec tria tenent, illi praedestinationem et praeteritionem sive reprobationem non ex praevisis hominum operationibus bonis malisque suspendunt, sed ex mera Dei voluntate miserentis cujus vult, et cujus non vult non miserentis: At Catholici illi qui Pelagianis et Semipelagianis sese opposuerunt, non minus quam ipse Augustinus haec tria axiomata propugnarunt: Ergo electionem et praeteritionem absolutam, et minime ex praevisa hominum fide et infidelitate, sive obedientia et contumacia pendulam statuerunt.
pass_a: Thus therefore this our reason stands: Those who preach and urge a certain special and efficacious grace, by which not only is the mind illuminated, the affections stirred, the will struck, so that by its benefit one can believe, repent, persevere, if he himself will, but by whose efficacy it always comes to pass that he wills; the will being healed, yea a new will created in the man, faith and charity inspired into the same, and perseverance given; and who acknowledge that such and so efficacious a grace has been prepared and given by God unto certain ones, unto others neither prepared nor given; finally, who teach that God decreed and gave that same special grace unto certain ones from his mere good pleasure, and not from antecedent regard unto diverse merits and demerits, or unto any contrary acts of men whatsoever, and unto others neither decreed it to be given nor gave it; who, I say, hold these three, they do not suspend predestination and preterition or reprobation from foresight of men’s operations good and evil, but from the mere will of God showing mercy on whom he wills, and not showing mercy on whom he wills not: But those Catholics who opposed themselves unto the Pelagians and Semipelagians defended these three axioms no less than Augustine himself: Therefore they established absolute election and preterition, and by no means hanging from foresight of men’s faith and unbelief, or obedience and contumacy.
pass_b: So our reason stands: Those who preach and press a special efficacious grace that not only lights the mind, stirs the affections, and knocks the will so that by its help one can believe, repent, and persevere if he wills, but by whose efficacy he always does will—the will healed, even a new will created, faith and charity breathed in, perseverance given; who confess such grace prepared and given by God to some, to others neither prepared nor given; and who teach that God decreed and gave that special grace to some from mere good pleasure, not from prior regard to diverse merits and demerits or any contrary human acts, and to others neither decreed nor gave it—those who hold these three do not hang predestination and preterition or reprobation on foresight of men’s good and evil workings, but on the mere will of God who has mercy on whom he wills and withholds mercy from whom he wills not. But the catholics who opposed Pelagians and Semipelagians defended these three axioms no less than Augustine. Therefore they set absolute election and preterition, not hanging on foresight of men’s faith and unbelief, or obedience and stubbornness.

lemmas.lemma: gratiam ... specialem et efficacem ... ut velit

lemmas.gloss: axiom 2: prepared for some not others
